items.summary: Abstract Sānér establishes a recursive control architecture for task regions by placing topology, self-modeling scheduling, and certificate-governed execution under one executable resource semantics. The nine-node construction supports exact recursive expansion and addressing. Its formal system establishes capacity safety, deterministic cross-layer selection, partition safety, conditional liveness, and computable deadline and recovery bounds. Using entity-isolated validation and one-time test splits, we evaluated the shared kernels and domain adapters in executable state-transition simulations and public benchmark workloads over 32–64 independent worlds, with deployment evidence obtained from 48 physical GPU blocks and eight fresh process pairs in the official Kubernetes scheduler-performance harness. Shared kernels with explicit domain realizations established task-level all-comparator superiority, while matched Kubernetes execution established a throughput advantage over the official default scheduler. The recursive representation preserved exact adjacency with a small measured footprint as graph size increased. Mechanism evidence remains separate from direct performance claims. Boundary results and nonidentifiability tests are reported independently. Together, the proofs and matched comparisons establish Sānér as a reusable and auditable control architecture whose shared mechanisms transfer across structurally different systems tasks. Validation design The study reports 52 simulation tasks and two deployment endpoints. Simulation comparisons use matched frozen worlds, observable information, action spaces, resource ceilings, and decision-time budgets. The Kubernetes deployment uses fresh paired processes under the same official scheduling and binding boundaries. Independent-unit inference, primary endpoints, and comparison procedures follow the recorded experimental contracts. Task-level all-comparator conclusions require passage against every member of the specified comparator family. Suite-defined Holm or FDR adjustments control multiplicity. Direct performance, mechanism validation, boundary results, and nonidentifiability remain separate evidence classes. Comparator strength and field standing Comparator selection was deliberately demanding. The experiments include established scheduling methods, matched MPC and CP-SAT, public MAPF implementations, official Kubernetes scheduling, strong decentralized-learning algorithms, and mature domain-specific methods. Every direct comparison uses matched information and resources. Executed comparator implementations are identified precisely. The consensus experiment uses a HotStuff three-chain simulation and a validation-tuned partition-threshold selector. The distribution-estimation experiment uses a discounted-loss context-depth KT mixture alongside Bayesian online changepoint prediction and discounted KT estimation. Published BFTBrain and context-tree weighting provide the corresponding methodological lineages. Results overview Sānér established task-level all-comparator superiority across 38 simulation tasks. Representative findings include a 764.53% improvement over equal-degree expander control, a 208.90% improvement over Exact Diffusion, and a 33.40% improvement over the Graph500 top-down port. At 5,000 nodes, the topology-based placement adapter sustained 69,258 placements per second. Under matched official Kubernetes execution, Sānér achieved 892.80 placements per second versus 371.19 for the default scheduler, with a mean paired throughput ratio of 2.40. Exact recursive-topology representation preserved neighbor recovery at 508–716 measured bytes through 26,244 nodes. Complete self-modeling was measured independently. The full experimental result index is provided in the Additional Description. Confirmatory scope The 38 task-level conclusions cover their complete specified strong-comparator families. items.summary: Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) is a fundamental inverse problem in geophysics to estimate subsurface properties, such as velocity, from seismic measurements. Recently, self-supervised learning methods remove the need for ground-truth velocity maps during training by leveraging a forward operator to simulate seismic data from predictions and backpropagate the gradients of reconstruction loss through it. In this work, we consider a more challenging setting without accessing such gradients. To this end, we incorporate reinforcement learning into self-supervised FWI and propose a framework named DeepWaveRL. Specifically, we reformulate FWI as a policy learning problem, where the policy network predicts velocity maps as actions, and a forward operator is used solely for simulation. A global scalar reward is computed based on data misfit for each prediction and used to weight policy gradients. Thus, learning proceeds without accessing the gradients from the forward operator. Given the indirect and coarse supervision signals, we further identify key strategies to stabilize learning and mitigate the spatial credit assignment bottleneck. Experimental results show that, despite relying entirely on a single scalar reward, DeepWaveRL achieves competitive performance compared to supervised and self-supervised baselines. These findings suggest that our framework offers a flexible and complementary learning paradigm for the FWI research community.
items.title: DeepWaveRL: Self-Supervised Full Waveform Inversion via Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Graph forecasters for sensor networks are trained in one regime and deployed in others, where sensor coupling and signal frequency content both change. We split this spectral shift into an operator channel and a frequency channel, each with a dimensionless measure. ST-GFM (Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting Model) filters every input step with Chebyshev and bidirectional diffusion filters on one learned, non-symmetric operator and alternates them with per-node temporal attention. For the operator channel we prove Frobenius-norm perturbation bounds for both graph branches, show that the Chebyshev bound is attained to first order, and compute its constant from the trained weights and the measured operator norm: 17.9 on METR-LA and 21.5 on PEMS-BAY. Under random edge dropout the trained layer moves by 2.0% to 3.1% of this bound. Masked Spectral Reconstruction (MSR), a self-supervised loss active in the first 40 epochs, matches the log power spectrum of the encoder output to that of the input. For small log-spectral residuals on unclamped bins it is proportional to an Itakura-Saito divergence to leading order. Removing it raises the 60-minute MAE by 0.30 on METR-LA, close to the 0.33 lost when all three self-supervised losses go. Under one shared evaluation pipeline, the 60-minute MAE of ST-GFM is 3.5% below a retrained STAEformer on METR-LA and 13.0% below it on PEMS-BAY. Its 60-minute MAE is 3.0980.017 on METR-LA (five seeds) and 1.5760.006 on PEMS-BAY (three seeds), the lowest PEMS-BAY MAE among twelve published baselines.

items.summary: High-dimensional data from multiple sources often combine shared structure with source-specific variation. We study heterogeneous principal component analysis, which seeks to recover common and private principal subspaces when their dimensions are unknown. {We propose \emph{Feature Extraction (FE)}, a novel data-driven framework with two steps. First, the Eigenvector-based Spike-Count (ESC) estimator determines the number of principal components (PC) in each source using only sample eigenvector information, rather than eigenvalue-based criteria. Second, FE identifies the locations of common features by comparing bias-corrected inner products between sample eigenvectors across sources. These matches yield estimates of the common and source-specific subspaces without iterative optimization. We establish the consistency of our estimators under a spiked covariance model in a high-dimensional regime where the dimension and sample size grow proportionally. Simulations and applications to federated image data and U.S. housing prices demonstrate the performance of FE in rank recovery, subspace estimation, and data reconstruction.} Code is available at https://github.com/liwenbo-research/HeterogeneousPCA
items.title: Features Extraction Across Multi-Source Heterogeneous Data

items.summary: LLM agents repeatedly send a growing conversation to a model, making prefix reuse central to efficient serving. We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. On SGLang, a ten-minute surge reduced goodput by about 88% over the following hour. Removing the residual burst sessions restored service within minutes. The sustaining mechanism is population-cache feedback. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. A fluid model identifies the resource conditions for this feedback and explains how cache capacity, tool time and base load affect vulnerability. Across 36 simulated deployments, it flags all 17 cache-first cases. Controlled simulations hold the post-surge state fixed and show that changing subsequent arrivals alone reverses the recovery outcome. Once the cache collapses, low-reuse departure capacity sets the scale of the load reduction needed for recovery. Guided by these dynamics, we build Basin, which gives each session a fixed priority, reserves their predicted peak contexts against an adaptive admission budget, extends the cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand. On real H200 1P3D deployments under surges, including long-context SWE-bench Pro sessions, an arrival-time prototype achieves 1.20--1.70x the goodput of Continuum and 2.35--3.59x that of HiCache alone. In simulation, the predictor-driven policy delivers 1.20--2.05x the strongest baseline's goodput across six surge scenarios.
items.title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving

items.summary: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.
items.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?

items.summary: A causal video generator produces two key--value (KV) states for every segment: the KV it uses while denoising that segment, and the KV it writes into the cache for later segments to read. In a pretrained generator the two already differ substantially, later segments attend to them differently, and replacing the written KV with the generation KV degrades the continuation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV) to learn a dedicated memory representation from its future use: a writer-specific low-rank residual on the shared backbone separates memory writing from generation and is trained through the future reads of what it writes. Learning a write from its future use needs gradients through the cache, which the mutable cache in common use cannot provide. dKV Forcing replaces the training-time cache by persistent differentiable pages with local rematerialization and, in one temporal traversal, computes exactly the gradient that a two-pass reconstruction of the same objective computes. One traversal computes the full memory gradient at $7\%$ generator-update overhead over detached-write training, with $28\%$ less resident memory and $20.8\%$ shorter training cycles than the two-pass reconstruction. Over Self Gradient Forcing (SGF), the same objective trained with the same traversal, writer adaptation raises VBench-Long aesthetic quality by $6.6$ points at 60\,s and $8.5$ points at 240\,s with the highest subject and background consistency, and rollout dropout of the residual keeps most of this gain while restoring the motion of training without write gradients.
items.title: dKV Forcing: Separating Generation and Memory Representations through a Differentiable KV Cache

items.summary: Measured failure modes of verifier panels: companion paper accepted (poster) at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop Who Verifies the Agents? — Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels . Version of record: SSRN 7390698 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7390698 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://polyhelper.ai/research/agreement-not-evidence/ and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/agreement-not-evidence . Someone who asks one language model a question cannot tell a confidently wrong answer from a confidently right one. The two are identical on every surface cue available to a non-expert. Asking several models seems to solve this, but it mostly relocates the problem: reconciling several answers produces one confident text again, and that text now carries the borrowed authority of "ten of them agreed." The protocol formalized here collects answers from several consumer chat models through the user's own browser or phone, with no API keys, no installation and no intermediary server. It reconciles them by anchor-and-enrich: the strongest available answer becomes the base, and each of the others contributes only what the base lacks. Every contribution is signed with the model that supplied it. Disagreements are kept in a section of their own rather than averaged away. The paper makes four contributions. The first is the protocol itself, stated as an algorithm that preserves provenance and forbids silent deletion, together with a taxonomy of five ways a merge can fail. Four of them are defects of naive pooling; the fifth is a failure of the operator rather than of the method: a synthesis that presents a single model's output as a collegial result. The second is the application of the correlated-witness arithmetic to protocol design. That arithmetic is not claimed here. Kohli (2026) applied the same Kish correction to a panel of nine frontier judges and measured about two effective votes, and Kim et al. (2025) established the underlying error correlation across more than 350 models. A council of N models whose errors carry intraclass correlation ρ is worth = N / (1 + (N−1)ρ) independent witnesses, and that quantity saturates at 1/ρ however many models are added. Once a council is larger than 1/ρ, halving ρ beats doubling N, and a pair with low error correlation can outweigh five with high correlation. Which pairs those are is measured, not read off the label: the larger and more accurate models carry the most correlated errors even when architecture and provider differ (Kim et al., 2025), and the author's per-pair measurements found no detectable effect of geopolitical bloc on error correlation and, in the pairs measured, none of shared lineage (Chernets, 2026). The estimation procedure of Section 5.5 supplies that measurement. The third is an account of three deployment tiers, manual, one-tap mobile and browser-agent, and of the axis that separates them epistemically: whether the second model sees the first model's answer. Conditioning the second model raises ρ in exchange for error correction. The fourth is a small-sample observation of the counterfeit-council failure across five models, the one-sentence intervention that removed it in a three-model re-run, and a blinded three-arm evaluation design with a stated falsification condition. Correlated agreement is treated here as established, not as a finding. That a panel of models is worth far fewer independent witnesses than it has members has been measured directly: nine frontier judges drawn from seven families supply about two effective votes (Kohli, 2026), and error correlation rises with model capability even across providers and architectures (Kim et al., 2025). Section 5 restates the design-effect arithmetic behind those measurements, because three of the protocol's rules are derived from it and read as fastidiousness without it. items.summary: SMaRT Transfusion  (Simplified, Meaningful and Responsible Tool for Transfusions) is a clinical decision support (CDS) tool developed at  Stanford Medicine Children's Health (SMCH)  for red blood cell (RBC) transfusion in critically ill children. It implements the consensus recommendations of the  Pediatric Critical Care Transfusion and Anemia eXpertise Initiative (TAXI) as an interactive decision tree: clinicians navigate from the patient's clinical state (hemorrhagic shock, nonhemorrhagic shock, acute respiratory failure, acute brain injury, hematologic/oncologic diagnoses, congenital or acquired heart disease, extracorporeal support, and general critical illness) through the relevant hemoglobin and physiologic thresholds to an evidence- or expert-based transfusion recommendation. It is designed for use within Epic and other EHR environments and accepts a hemoglobin value on launch to pre-seed the pathway.
items.title: SMaRT Transfusion: A Clinical Decision Support Tool for Red Blood Cell Transfusion in Critically Ill Children

items.summary: Sensor fusion, data fusion, dashboards and data visualisation are conventionally distinguished by input type and by where they sit in a processing stack. This paper argues that the distinction which matters for decision quality is a different one, and that it is two variables applied to all four: every representation of multi-source evidence collapses a distribution somewhere between sensor and decision, and representations differ in the locus of that collapse and in whether the residual uncertainty survives it as a carried object. Fusion collapses upstream and, when honest, ships the residual as covariance or hypothesis mass. Dashboards defer collapse to the viewer's retina and ship nothing; the resulting belief has no bookkeeping. Visualisation is the encoding of whichever object arrives, indifferent to whether it is a point or a distribution, which is why it is blamed for collapses committed upstream. The two variables, collapse locus and residual retention, place the four terms on one map, generalise the confabulation coefficient of The Confabulating Collator from language-model collators to the whole representation stack, and yield a diagnostic: the failure mode conventionally called bad fusion is a product that collapsed upstream and discarded its residual, delivering the confidence of a posterior with the epistemic hygiene of a gauge. The publicly reported expectation, in the investigation of the February 2026 Minab strike, that a targeting platform would have flagged contradictions it carried no representation of, is read as this failure at operational scale, with the causal question left where the public record leaves it. A design rule follows: defer collapse to the human where the human carries the prior the system lacks, fuse where they do not, and at neither locus discard the residual. The constructive requirement for language-level fusion products is stated and handed to a companion paper on divergence retention. The operator located in the architecture is Binary Bias.

items.summary: Wave energy converters (WECs) are typically designed to operate near resonance to maximize energy capture. While this enhances power absorption, it also amplifies structural loads and accelerates fatigue damage. As a result, fatigue becomes a critical design driver even when stress remains below material yield limits. Fatigue in offshore systems has been widely studied, particularly under variable-amplitude loading induced by waves, wind, and currents. These effects are commonly evaluated using the Palmgren–Miner damage accumulation rule, where failure is predicted once cumulative damage reaches unity. However, fatigue assessment for WECs remains less developed, especially in terms of linking environmental conditions to structural degradation and operational stress limits. The objective of this work is to evaluate, predict and improve confidence in the structural response and fatigue life of a WEC under representative operating conditions and to identify critical components and failure modes before deployment in March 2026 accounting for not only load and geometric factors, but also environmental conditions such as temperature.
items.title: Worst-Case Fatigue Life of an OSWEC Under Sustained Sea States

items.summary: Classical creative-process orderings put divergence early and convergence late, and the Double Diamond formalises the rule twice over. This paper argues the ordering was never a law of cognition but a map of costs: divergence goes early because reopening a converged process has historically been ruinous, and the entire discipline of the framework exists to protect against that reopening. When drafting cost collapses by orders of magnitude, as it does when an author works with a language model as typewriter, the protected assumption dissolves and the optimal ordering inverts: converge first, then diverge, because a late horizon either restarts a now-cheap process or spawns a child concept from a sharpened parent. The paper's second claim types reviewer instances in multi-model chains by regression target rather than capability, and states the Hein Condition: a mode-regressing reviewer's yield is proportional to the sharpness of the artefact it receives, because the modal response to an unsharp artefact is the generic response, so the same instance is most fluent exactly where it is least useful. A slot theory follows, carnivore, auditor, mode-regressor, children, each reviewer placed where its failure mode is cheapest, and child viability rises with parent sharpness at spawn. The claims are exercised on a fully documented case: a five-pass, three-model review chain run on a single paper in a single day, with every absorption, declination, and provenance failure logged. Four predictions close, including that review chains are provenance systems measurable by the sibling paper's key-inflation ratio.

items.summary: Binary Bias (Temte 2026a) claims that the collapse of continuous, conditional and multi-valued phenomena into sealed either/or categories is a substrate from which other catalogued biases grow. The claim has so far been argued, not counted. This paper specifies an audit that counts it: a random sample of 3,000 journal-article abstracts drawn through Crossref's sampling endpoint, enriched with field and era metadata from OpenAlex, and coded for binary collapse by three independent language-model coders with ten percent human double-coding. The coding scheme separates four loci at which a binary can sit (territory, design, inference, format), scores severity on a 0 to 5 Boolikert rather than as present or absent, and counts the sealing of a null result into an absence claim (nulsegl) as its own category. An evening-scale pilot of twenty abstracts, reported in full, motivates six hypotheses with pre-stated effect sizes: that inference- and format-locus collapse appears in at least a quarter of abstracts; that the format locus dominates in clinical literature and the inference locus in social and policy literature; that nulsegl is the single most frequent collapse type; that fields whose core object is already a ratio collapse less than fields whose core object is a category; that the 2016 statement on p-values changed vocabulary rather than verdicts; and that abstracts collapse more than the discussion sections they summarise. Publication of the protocol before the data is the pre-registration; the result is published whichever way it falls.

items.summary: Bridges are critical transportation infrastructure, and reliable operation and maintenance (O&M) is essential for traffic safety and long-term structural performance. However, bridge O&M faces key bottlenecks: no unified architecture coordinates heterogeneous resources; model inferences lack clear links to physical-mechanical laws; and experts' tacit knowledge remains difficult to formalize. This study proposes a knowledge-enhanced autonomy formalization methodology and apply it to construct the Bridge O&M Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System (BOMMA), which integrates heterogeneous diagnostic actions, physics-mechanics-informed representations, long-term memory, and structured experiential knowledge within a coordinated multi-agent workflow, enabling interpretable and traceable scheduling, analysis, and decision-making. On 3,492 multi-source instructions, the proposed method achieves scheduling recalls of 85.37% for simple and 99.40% for composite tasks, with 95.35% BERT F1-score for O&M action reasoning. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of the components in the autonomy. This study bridges general LLM reasoning and specialized bridge O&M requirements.
items.title: Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System for Bridge Operation and Maintenance based on Large Language Model

items.summary: Abstract Sānér establishes a recursive control architecture for task regions by placing topology, self-modeling scheduling, and certificate-governed execution under one executable resource semantics. The nine-node construction supports exact recursive expansion and addressing. Its formal system establishes capacity safety, deterministic cross-layer selection, partition safety, conditional liveness, and computable deadline and recovery bounds. Using entity-isolated validation and one-time test splits, we evaluated the shared kernels and domain adapters in executable state-transition simulations and public benchmark workloads over 32–64 independent worlds, with deployment evidence obtained from 48 physical GPU blocks and eight fresh process pairs in the official Kubernetes scheduler-performance harness. Shared kernels with explicit domain realizations established task-level all-comparator superiority, while matched Kubernetes execution established a throughput advantage over the official default scheduler. The recursive representation preserved exact adjacency with a small measured footprint as graph size increased. Mechanism evidence remains separate from direct performance claims. Boundary results and nonidentifiability tests are reported independently. Together, the proofs and matched comparisons establish Sānér as a reusable and auditable control architecture whose shared mechanisms transfer across structurally different systems tasks. Validation design The study reports 52 simulation tasks and two deployment endpoints. Simulation comparisons use matched frozen worlds, observable information, action spaces, resource ceilings, and decision-time budgets. The Kubernetes deployment uses fresh paired processes under the same official scheduling and binding boundaries. Independent-unit inference, primary endpoints, and comparison procedures follow the recorded experimental contracts. Task-level all-comparator conclusions require passage against every member of the specified comparator family. Suite-defined Holm or FDR adjustments control multiplicity. Direct performance, mechanism validation, boundary results, and nonidentifiability remain separate evidence classes. Comparator strength and field standing Comparator selection was deliberately demanding. The experiments include established scheduling methods, matched MPC and CP-SAT, public MAPF implementations, official Kubernetes scheduling, strong decentralized-learning algorithms, and mature domain-specific methods. Every direct comparison uses matched information and resources. Executed comparator implementations are identified precisely. The consensus experiment uses a HotStuff three-chain simulation and a validation-tuned partition-threshold selector. The distribution-estimation experiment uses a discounted-loss context-depth KT mixture alongside Bayesian online changepoint prediction and discounted KT estimation. Published BFTBrain and context-tree weighting provide the corresponding methodological lineages. Results overview Sānér established task-level all-comparator superiority across 38 simulation tasks. Representative findings include a 764.53% improvement over equal-degree expander control, a 208.90% improvement over Exact Diffusion, and a 33.40% improvement over the Graph500 top-down port. items.summary: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
items.title: KlaskTron: An Open-Source Platform for Physical Adversarial Multi-Agent RL

items.summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
items.title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design

items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliable application to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results naturally lead to ZO-BOLT, which applies ZO optimization to BOLT's RLVR-aligned weighted-SFT objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three model variants and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.
items.title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.
items.title: AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding

items.summary: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.
items.title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations

items.summary: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.
items.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?

items.summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.
items.title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game

items.summary: Version 1.02, 3 November 2026. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) estimate that one additional industrial robot per thousand workers lowers a U.S. local labor market's employment-to-population ratio by 0.39 percentage points and its hourly wages by about 0.77 percent. Rebuilding their design from raw IPUMS, IFR, and EU KLEMS data, I reproduce these estimates bit-exactly. I then ask what conventional robustness checks leave open: which industries, places, periods, and shocks actually identify the estimate? The regression spans 722 commuting zones and 19 industries, but the variation behind an instrumental-variable estimate can be far narrower. The sign is robust; the support is narrow. Negative estimates persist across conventional specification changes, 60 strong European instrument windows, alternative U.S. treatment windows, and the published periods through 2014. Yet automotive carries about 84 percent of normalized absolute Rotemberg-weight mass, and automotive exposure in six Rust Belt states supplies 95 percent of the net first-stage covariance. Without automotive, the remaining 18 industry shocks do not strongly predict U.S. robot exposure. Longer horizons, later start years, and adding Germany to the instrument all strengthen it through the same margin. The automotive component shows no detectable relation to 1970–1990 employment and wage changes, and a direct effect of the instrument would have to absorb 72 percent of the reduced form before conventional significance disappears. Inference is weaker than the regional first stage suggests. With 19 underlying industry shocks, exposure-robust first-stage F-statistics are 6.2 and 6.3 rather than 34, small-sample Anderson–Rubin tests do not reject a zero effect ( p = 0.059, 0.063), and other implementations of the same test disagree; in known-truth simulations, nominal 95-percent state-clustered intervals cover in only 60–66 percent of replications. Measurement assumptions also bind. In the original penetration metric, perpetual-inventory robot capital preserves the estimates at 5 percent depreciation, but faster assumed depreciation counts the automotive installations behind the first stage as replacement rather than net additions, eliminating shock-level relevance at 10 percent and all relevance at 15 percent. The benchmark is reproducible and robust in sign, but it is identified from an automotive margin in historically industrial labor markets; that margin defines its scope and the concrete content of its exclusion restriction. More generally, coefficient robustness and breadth of identifying support are distinct properties that shift-share studies should report separately. JEL Codes: J23, J24, O33, R23, C18, C26 Keywords: Industrial robots; automation; replication; shift-share IV; Bartik instruments; Rotemberg weights; identifying support; weak-instrument-robust inference; Anderson–Rubin; plausibly exogenous; perpetual inventory; robot capital; local labor markets
items.title: Robots and Jobs Revisited: A Bit-Exact Replication, Shift-Share Anatomy, and Capital-Stock Extension of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020)

items.summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), and they introduce the risk of coordination among agents that might escape human oversight. The J-space has been used to uncover deception in single LLMs, but its use for uncovering and steering collusion between agents remains unexplored. We show, with interpretability experiments on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) on the NARCBench collusion benchmark, that colluding agents' J-space holds the collusion itself: before replying, 86% of colluders represent misrepresentation, concealment or remorse. In a steganographic card-counting task, the receiver's J-space holds a hidden count, and causal interventions alter its count. We also introduce the Jacobian Pair Contrast (J-PACT), an unsupervised method for detecting collusion between agents. We evaluate J-PACT on four open-weight models: GPT-OSS-20B, Llama-3.3-70B-IT, Qwen3-32B, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B). J-PACT retains 85% of the above-chance AUROC of supervised NARCBench probes, matches them on steganographic scenarios, and names the colluding pair up to its complement in 99% of detected runs.
items.title: Multi-Agent Collusion and the J-Space

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.
items.title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks

items.summary: Replication package for the empirical study "Who Migrates the Schema? An Empirical Study of Database Changes in AI Coding Agent Pull Requests" (submitted to Empirical Software Engineering). The study analyses what AI coding agents (OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code, Google Jules) do in the database layer (migrations, DDL, ORM schemas, raw SQL) of GitHub pull requests, and compares them with human pull requests from the same 889 database-bearing repositories and the same period (2024-12-24 to 2025-10-24). The package contains (i) code.zip: the frozen detector specification, mining code, human-baseline collector, independent re-implementation, statistical analysis (Python and R), revision analyses, all output tables and the human-validation labels; (ii) data.zip: sanitised per-PR and per-file derived tables sufficient to re-run the statistical analysis. GitHub person logins are pseudonymised (HMAC-SHA256 with a secret salt); bot and agent accounts are kept because they define the treatment. Patch text, PR titles/bodies and comments are not redistributed; scripts to re-collect them are included. Agent-side tables derive from the AIDev dataset (hao-li/AIDev, MSR '26; CC BY 4.0).
items.title: Replication package for "Who Migrates the Schema? An Empirical Study of Database Changes in AI Coding Agent Pull Requests"

items.summary: Large language model applications are increasingly being organized as tool-using and multi-agent workflows rather than as isolated chat interfaces. This perspective paper examines the architectural problem that follows from that shift: agents may reason, invoke tools, and delegate work, but dependable deployment still requires interoperability across frameworks, runtimes, data boundaries, and organizational control domains. We study this problem through the lens of the \emph{Internet of Agentics} (IoA), an emerging service-computing view in which heterogeneous agents are treated as governable service participants rather than only as stand-alone model endpoints. The paper organizes the landscape as a three-layer progression: from today's fragmented agent ecosystem, to interoperable agents, and ultimately to trustworthy and governable autonomy. First, it examines the protocol stack centered on the Agentic AI Foundation, including MCP for agent--tool interaction; A2A for agent--agent coordination; AGENTS.md and Skills-style procedural manifests; and discovery, transport, and trust mechanisms such as AGNTCY and SLIM. Second, it reviews the systems abstractions that make agents deployable as service components, including logical agent architectures, orchestration patterns, gateways, registries, runtime control loops, and hardware-aware inference infrastructure. Third, it situates these developments within services computing, arguing that agentic systems reinterpret classical concerns from SOA and microservices---discovery, composition, governance, pricing, and trust---at the level of cognitive capabilities rather than deterministic functions.
items.title: Towards a Trustworthy and Governable Internet of Agentics: An Architectural Perspective on Protocols, Systems, and Services

items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate detailed video captions, yet they may overemphasize minor details while overlooking essential context and key events. We argue that not all visual evidence deserves equal attention, as the importance of visual information depends on the content of each video. Motivated by this observation, we propose Reviso, an agentic video captioning framework that learns what to observe and how to gather relevant visual evidence. From a low-frame-rate global preview, Reviso constructs a hierarchical Context--Focus--Points (CFP) observation plan that identifies the video context, prioritizes key aspects, and defines concrete observation targets and corresponding tools. Guided by this plan, Reviso performs goal-directed active perception by selectively revisiting temporal segments and combining tools for fine-grained inspection. It interprets the acquired evidence, updates its plan as needed, and integrates global and local information to generate the final caption. To learn this observation strategy, we develop a verification-guided pipeline that constructs high-quality training trajectories through factual verification and teacher-guided refinement. We further train Reviso using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), incorporating a key-fact reward for caption quality, a Plan Alignment Reward (PAR) for identifying important observation targets, and an Unproductive Tool-Call Penalty (UTCP) that adjusts observation-cost penalties based on caption quality. Experiments across four video captioning benchmarks show that Reviso outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines, while its generated captions better support downstream video question answering. These findings highlight the effectiveness and potential of priority-guided active observation for video captioning.
items.title: Reviso: Not All Visual Evidence Deserves Equal Attention in Video Captioning

items.summary: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
items.title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue

items.summary: The Sundarbans mangrove system constitutes a globally consequential blue carbon sink, yet vertically resolved soil organic carbon (SOC) inventories, particularly at depth, remain under-constrained. This study deployed a geospatial deep-learning pipeline integrating multi-source Earth observation data (optical, SAR, and DEM-derived covariates) to spatially upscale SOC stocks to 1 m depth across the Bangladesh Sundarbans. Stratified coring across five sites positioned along the salinity–tidal inundation gradient to represent four major vegetation zones (n = 25; one pit per site × five depth intervals: 0–20, 20–40, 40–60, 60–80, 80–100 cm) captured physicochemical and SOC attributions. A Kruskal–Wallis test confirmed a positive SOC gradient with depth (H = 21.7, df = 4, p < 0.001); post-hoc Dunn’s pairwise comparisons showed 60–100 cm layers differed significantly from all shallower layers (p < 0.01, Bonferroni-adjusted), with the dominant pool residing below 40 cm, implying systematic underestimation by conventional shallow-core (<30–40 cm) assessments. To partition total ecosystem carbon and establish soil-pool dominance, above- and belowground biomass were parameterized using species-specific allometric equations, revealing high stem density but comparatively low basal area consistent with a regenerating stand structure dominated by Heritiera fomes and Sonneratia apetala. Analysis of a previously published Landsat-derived mangrove record (1988–2022) revealed net contraction in mangrove extent; loss-agent raster attribution, based on shoreline-proximity buffers, land-cover transition sequences and cyclone-track coincidence, identified chronic tidal abrasion and erosion as the primary driver rather than anthropogenic conversion or cyclonic disturbance. Benchmarking against a previously published global 30 m machine-learning SOC product revealed a 4.2-fold underestimation of SOC stocks in the Bangladesh Sundarbans, particularly in peat-enriched, anoxic substrata. Assimilation of deep-profile in situ observations with the pipeline significantly improves spatial prediction fidelity and establishes a robust baseline for Measurement, Reporting, and Verification for greenhouse gas inventories, highlighting the necessity of incorporating deep-soil carbon pools for inventorizing erosion-vulnerable seaward margins.
items.title: Blue Carbon Stock Mapping of the Sundarbans Mangrove Ecosystem, Bangladesh (2000–2025): A Hybrid GeoAI Ensemble Framework

items.summary: Language models in customer-facing products must be continually updated, since the data they serve shifts over time. As retraining on the full accumulated data is impractical, each update should instead run on a small set of examples carrying the training signal of all data seen so far. The strongest current methods build this set by gradient matching, which synthesizes examples whose training gradients match those of the full data. However, they require ground-truth labels, run once on a fixed snapshot rather than on a growing stream, and are slow on large data. We introduce \textbf{OLGA}, which lifts these limitations. It distills unlabeled data by drawing the gradient matching targets from the model's own next-token predictions. Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, it improves accuracy by 10 percentage points over the strongest selection baseline using as few as five examples. OLGA also distills online data streams by keeping a running rehearsal memory of synthetic examples, which is re-distilled together with each new batch as it arrives. In the online setting, it outperforms the strongest selection-based continual baseline by 6.6 stream-AUC percentage points. Finally, our method scales to large data by pairing distillation with selection in a hybrid pipeline, letting selection handle the mild stage of compression and distillation the extreme one. It cuts runtime by 30\% versus distillation alone at similar accuracy, and beats the best selection-only pipeline by up to 12.6 percentage points.
items.title: Online Label-Free Gradient Matching for Continual Language Model Training

items.summary: This repository contains the code and numerical data supporting the manuscript “Higher-Order Relational Assurance for Modular Autonomous System Architectures” by Juan J. Segura. The study investigates how much relational information modular system interfaces must preserve in order to reconstruct an integrated dynamic-admissibility relation. The reproducibility package contains Python source code, benchmark configuration files, and CSV datasets and outputs used for the principal computational analyses. The package supports two complementary model layers: (1) a reduced continuous-control model used for exhaustive higher-order project-join analysis and robustness studies, and (2) a synthetic seven-state road-relative vehicle model used as a nonlinear dynamic falsification layer. The principal reproducible results include: complete pairwise reconstruction providing no improvement over unary reconstruction; persistence of this pairwise insufficiency across 27 combinations of numerical resolution, superelevation, and stopping horizon; and a sparse ternary architecture comprising the relations {R, mu, v}, {G, mu, v}, and {mu, v, tau} reproducing the complete third-order reconstruction in all 27 robustness cases. The vehicle parameters are synthetic and are not presented as OEM-calibrated haul-truck data. All admissibility projections are exact only with respect to the computed model relation. The reported discordance measures should not be interpreted as accident probabilities or empirical risk frequencies.
items.title: Code and Data for Higher-Order Relational Assurance for Modular Autonomous System Architectures

items.summary: Long-horizon tasks require large language model (LLM) agents to coordinate interdependent actions, a capability central to automating complex workflows. Stepwise group-based reinforcement learning provides finer credit than trajectory-level supervision, but reliable comparisons must account for differences in interaction history. Enforcing this consistency within the limited rollouts of each task can leave insufficient support for estimating action preferences. We propose Beyond-Local Policy Optimization (BLPO), which estimates task-progress advantages from experience shared across tasks and training updates. We summarize trajectory prefixes into task-progress states and abstract actions by their function, allowing corresponding decisions from different tasks to contribute to shared estimates. To control bias and noise from heterogeneous tasks, we accumulate context-relative returns in a global memory with balanced aggregation and reliability weighting. These global advantages complement local comparisons over normalized actions and trajectory-level credit without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with 1.5B and 7B policies show improved task success over the evaluated baselines under matched training budgets. Further analyses show faster learning and shorter trajectories with little computational overhead.
items.title: BLPO: Beyond-Local Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

items.summary: LLM agents repeatedly send a growing conversation to a model, making prefix reuse central to efficient serving. We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. On SGLang, a ten-minute surge reduced goodput by about 88% over the following hour. Removing the residual burst sessions restored service within minutes. The sustaining mechanism is population-cache feedback. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. A fluid model identifies the resource conditions for this feedback and explains how cache capacity, tool time and base load affect vulnerability. Across 36 simulated deployments, it flags all 17 cache-first cases. Controlled simulations hold the post-surge state fixed and show that changing subsequent arrivals alone reverses the recovery outcome. Once the cache collapses, low-reuse departure capacity sets the scale of the load reduction needed for recovery. Guided by these dynamics, we build Basin, which gives each session a fixed priority, reserves their predicted peak contexts against an adaptive admission budget, extends the cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand. On real H200 1P3D deployments under surges, including long-context SWE-bench Pro sessions, an arrival-time prototype achieves 1.20--1.70x the goodput of Continuum and 2.35--3.59x that of HiCache alone. In simulation, the predictor-driven policy delivers 1.20--2.05x the strongest baseline's goodput across six surge scenarios.
items.title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving

items.summary: Abstract Background: Non-adherence to medication is a major barrier to achieving optimal health outcomes in chronic diseases. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a multi-component, pharmacist-led intervention in improving medication adherence and Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) among patients with diabetes and/or hypertension in India. Methods: A quasi-experimental pre-post design was employed. A subset of 120 participants with low adherence (MMAS-8 score <6) were recruited from a larger cross-sectional study. The intervention, delivered over 9 months, included patient education, digital reminders, and personalized counseling. Adherence (MMAS-8) and HRQoL (SF-36 PCS/MCS, WHOQOL-BREF) were measured at baseline, 3, 6, and 9 months. A control group (n=98) received standard care. Results: Of the 120 participants in the intervention group, 105 completed the 9-month follow-up. The intervention group showed significant improvements in adherence (MMAS-8 score increased from 4.2 ± 1.2 to 6.8 ± 1.2, p < 0.001). Significant improvements were also observed in PCS (46.2 ± 18.4 to 60.2 ± 16.2, p < 0.001), MCS (50.4 ± 19.2 to 62.4 ± 17.2, p < 0.001), and WHOQOL-BREF overall scores (48.6 ± 16.8 to 58.6 ± 15.4, p < 0.001). At 9 months, the intervention group demonstrated significantly better outcomes compared to the control group across all measures (p < 0.001 for all). Conclusions: The multi-component, pharmacist-led intervention was highly effective in improving both medication adherence and HRQoL in patients with chronic conditions. These findings support the integration of clinical pharmacists into chronic disease management teams in India to improve patient outcomes. Keywords  Medication Adherence, Health-Related Quality of Life, Pharmacist-Led Intervention, Patient Education, Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, India.
items.title: Effectiveness of a Multi-Component Pharmacist-Led Intervention on MA and HRQoL in Indian Patients with Chronic Diseases: A Quasi-Experimental Study
